title: Chat, API, agent, embedded feature
description: The four shapes AI actually takes in real software, and why "we added AI" can mean four completely different things depending on which one you mean.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish chat, API call, agent and embedded feature by who decides what to ask the model
Identify which pattern a real product or workflow is using

contentSections.title: Four different things wearing the same name

contentSections.body: A small business owner tells a friend, proudly, "we added AI to our website." The friend asks what it does. "You know — like ChatGPT." It is not like ChatGPT. There's no box to type into anywhere on the site. A customer fills in a contact form, and forty seconds later gets an oddly well-written reply. Somewhere behind that form, code is calling an AI provider directly — no conversation, no back-and-forth, just one request and one response, wired into a form submission. "Like ChatGPT" is doing a lot of work to cover four genuinely different things.

contentSections.scenario: A recruiter's applicant-tracking software has a button labelled "Summarise this CV." She clicks it. Ten seconds later, a three-line summary appears in the sidebar, in the same visual style as the rest of the software. She never sees a prompt, never sees a chat window, and can't see what instructions were sent to produce that summary.
contentSections.question: Which of the four patterns is this?

options.label: Chat interface
API call made by someone else's code
Agent, deciding its own steps
Embedded feature

feedback.chat: There's no conversation here — no back-and-forth, no box to type a follow-up into. That rules out chat, even though the underlying mechanism (a request to an AI model) is genuinely similar.
feedback.api: An API call is happening underneath this, but that's true of embedded features too — the API call is *how* the feature is built, not what the recruiter is experiencing. From where she's sitting, this is a button in her existing software, not a request she composed.
feedback.agent: Nothing here suggests multiple decisions or steps — one click, one summary, done. An agent would be doing something more like reading the CV, deciding it needs the job description too, fetching that, and combining both before responding.
feedback.embedded: Right. The AI is wired into a specific point in software that exists for another purpose — tracking applicants — with a button someone else designed, a prompt she'll never see, and behaviour she can't adjust beyond what that button offers. That's the defining feature of an embedded feature: you interact with a product, not with the model.

contentSections.concept: Four AI patterns: **chat** (a human converses directly with a model, turn by turn), **API call** (code sends a request, gets a response, no conversation), **agent** (a system takes a goal and decides its own sequence of steps, often calling tools along the way), **embedded feature** (AI wired into an existing product at one specific point, with the prompt and behaviour fixed by whoever built it).

contentSections.body: The distinction that actually matters isn't "does this use AI" — all four do. It's **who is deciding what to ask the model, and how often**. In chat, you decide, every single turn. In an API call, a developer decided once, when they wrote the code, and every request afterward follows that same fixed shape. In an agent, the system itself decides what to ask next, based on what came back from the last step — which is powerful and also the reason agents are the hardest of the four to predict. In an embedded feature, someone else decided, in advance, and you never see the decision at all — you just get the button.

This matters practically because the four patterns fail differently, and cost differently, and take different amounts of effort to build or use well. A chat conversation is the cheapest to start and the most flexible, but it needs a human present for every exchange — it can't run overnight. An API call can run unattended and produce a consistent shape of output, but someone has to build and maintain the code around it. An agent can handle a task nobody fully specified in advance, but it can also confidently do the wrong thing three steps in a row before a human notices, because nobody was checking each step. An embedded feature asks the least of you — no prompt to write, no code to run — but you get exactly the behaviour the product shipped with, and nothing more.

contentSections.code: Team decision, as written in a planning doc: "We'll use an AI agent for the customer refund process. The agent will read the complaint, check the order history, decide the refund amount, and issue it automatically, so no one on the team needs to review refunds day to day."
contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw in this plan — not "AI is risky" in general, but the specific thing this plan gets wrong?

options.text: Agents can't check order history, only chat interfaces can look things up
It hands financial decisions to a multi-step, self-directed process with no human check on any individual step
Refunds should never involve AI in any form

feedback.cant-lookup: Agents are specifically built to call tools — looking up order history is exactly the kind of step an agent can do. That's not the problem here.
feedback.no-check: Right. The plan's real flaw isn't using an agent — it's removing every human checkpoint from a process that moves money, on a pattern (the agent) that is specifically the one most likely to compound a wrong decision across several steps before anyone sees it.
feedback.never-ai: AI genuinely can help triage or draft refund decisions well; the issue isn't the presence of AI, it's the absence of any review point in a process with real financial consequences.

contentSections.flawExplanation: Agents are the pattern with the least human involvement per step, by design — that's what makes them useful for complex, multi-stage tasks. It's also exactly why handing one full authority over money, with literally nobody checking any individual decision, is the highest-risk way to use that pattern. The fix isn't to avoid agents for this; it's to keep a human review step — an agent that drafts a refund recommendation for someone to approve is a completely different risk profile from one that issues it.

contentSections.body: The four patterns aren't a ladder of "better AI" — they're different answers to "who decides what to ask the model, and when," and picking the right one for a job matters more than picking the newest one.
Take one ordinary task — writing a short thank-you note to a client after a project wraps — and watch it become four different jobs depending on which pattern handles it.

contentSections.problem: Draft a thank-you note to a client, "Priya," after finishing a three-week logo design project, in a warm but professional tone.

steps.label: As chat
steps.work: You open a chat window and type: "Write a warm, professional thank-you note to a client named Priya after wrapping up a 3-week logo design project. Mention we're happy to help with future brand work." You read the reply, tweak one line, copy it into your email.
steps.why: You're present for the whole exchange and can redirect it instantly if it's off — the cost is that you have to be there, typing, every single time you send one of these.

steps.label: As an API call
steps.work: A developer writes a small program: whenever a project in your project-management tool is marked "complete," the program automatically sends the client's name and project type to an AI provider's API with a fixed instruction template, and pastes the response into a draft email for you to send.
steps.why: It runs without you typing anything, every time, consistently — but someone had to build and maintain that program, and it only handles exactly the situation it was written for.

steps.label: As an embedded feature
steps.work: Your project-management software itself has a built-in "Draft closing email" button that appears when a project is marked complete. You click it. Someone at that software company designed the prompt, the tone, and the trigger — you have no way to see or adjust the actual instructions being sent.
steps.why: Zero setup, zero maintenance — and zero control beyond whatever settings the button exposes. If it always sounds slightly too stiff for your brand, you can't fix that; you can only stop using the button.

steps.label: As an agent
steps.work: You give a system a broader goal — "handle client offboarding for completed projects" — and it decides on its own to draft the thank-you note, check the invoice was paid before sending it, and hold the note if payment is still outstanding.
steps.why: It's handling a goal, not a single fixed task, deciding its own steps along the way — useful when the real job is genuinely multi-step, overkill and harder to audit when it's really just one email.

faded.problem: Same task — a thank-you note after a project — but now the client relationship is ongoing (Priya sends you work every few months) and you want the note to also flag your current availability for new projects.

blanks.prompt: If you wanted this handled with zero setup and you're willing to accept whatever tone the software ships with, which pattern do you reach for?
blanks.why: Zero setup is the whole trade embedded features offer — you give up control over the exact wording in exchange for not building or maintaining anything.

blanks.prompt: If the availability note needs to check your actual calendar before saying anything about being available — a genuine multi-step decision — which pattern actually fits that?
blanks.why: Checking a calendar and then deciding what to say based on the result is exactly the kind of multi-step, self-directed sequence agents are for — an API call alone would need a human to already know the calendar answer before triggering it.

faded.procedure: Ask what's actually varying between requests (nothing → API call is enough; genuinely multi-step → agent), then ask who needs to be present (nobody → not chat; the software vendor already built it → embedded).

contentSections.body: Notice that none of the four is objectively "the best" version of this task — they trade control for effort in opposite directions. Chat gives you the most control and costs the most of your ongoing time. The embedded feature costs almost none of your time and gives you almost no control. The API call and the agent sit in between, and differ from each other mainly in how much the system is deciding on its own versus following a script someone wrote once. Lesson five comes back to this trade-off directly; for now, the useful habit is just noticing which one you're looking at.

contentSections.title: "Just add AI to the returns page"
contentSections.opening: A small online shop's owner asks you to "add AI to the returns page" so customers get instant answers about whether an item qualifies for return.

assess.situation: You need to figure out what she actually needs before picking a pattern.
assess.question: What's the first thing worth finding out?

choices.label: How many return questions actually come in per week
choices.consequence: Good instinct — volume tells you whether a manual or embedded solution is even worth it.

choices.label: Which AI provider has the best marketing
choices.consequence: That's a real question eventually, but it's premature — you don't know what you're building yet.

volume.situation: Turns out it's about 30 return questions a week, and the rules (14-day window, item must be unworn, a few category exceptions) are fixed and rarely change.
volume.question: Given fixed rules and steady, moderate volume, which pattern fits best?

choices.label: An embedded feature or a simple API-driven FAQ widget — fixed rules, no need for anything self-directed
choices.consequence: Right call. Fixed rules and steady volume are exactly what a consistent, single-request pattern handles well — no need for an agent deciding its own steps.

choices.label: A full agent that can look up each order, negotiate exceptions, and issue refunds autonomously
choices.consequence: That's a lot of self-directed authority for a task whose rules don't actually change — more moving parts than the job needs, and more ways for it to go wrong unsupervised.

good.summary: A fixed-rule, moderate-volume FAQ task matched to a simple, predictable pattern.
good.lesson: The simplest pattern that reliably does the job is usually right — lesson five names this directly.

costly.summary: An agent with real authority over refunds, built for a task that didn't need self-directed decision-making at all.
costly.lesson: More autonomous patterns aren't more impressive — they're appropriate only when the task genuinely requires deciding its own next step.

contentSections.body: Before asking "which AI tool should I use," ask "which of these four shapes does my task actually need" — the answer is rarely the most sophisticated one.

title: What an API call actually is
description: The plain-English mechanics of an API call — what's sent, where it goes, what comes back, and why it creates an ongoing dependency rather than a one-time install.

learningObjectives.text: Describe what happens, mechanically, in an API request and response
Recognise an API-related failure as a provider-side issue rather than a code bug

contentSections.title: What's actually being sent, and back

contentSections.body: A shop owner gets a quote from a developer: "$400 to add AI product descriptions, plus about two cents per description after that." She asks, reasonably, what the two cents is actually paying for — there's no subscription, no app, nothing installed. Just... two cents, per description, forever.

contentSections.question: Before the explanation: what do you think physically happens between clicking "generate description" and the text appearing — where does the actual work happen?
contentSections.answer: The click sends a request over the internet to the AI provider's own servers (not the shop's website, not the shop owner's computer), where the model actually runs; the provider's server sends the generated text back, and that's what appears on the page. The shop's website never runs the model itself — it just asks and receives.
contentSections.hint: The shop's website is small and cheap to host. Running a large AI model takes an enormous amount of computing power. Where does that power actually live?

contentSections.body: An API call, stripped of jargon, is three things: a **request** (some text — instructions plus whatever specific content, like a product name and a few bullet points), an **address** it gets sent to (the provider's server, over the internet, the same way a web page request goes to a website's server), and a **response** (text that comes back, usually a few seconds later). The "key" a developer mentions is just an account credential — it proves the request is coming from a paying account, the same way a login proves who you are. Nothing about this involves installing a program or downloading the model; the model stays on the provider's servers the entire time, which is also why the description costs money every time it runs, rather than once.

This is also why an API-driven feature can go quietly wrong in ways a chat window doesn't. In a chat window, if something's off, you see it immediately and can just ask again. In an embedded, automated request-response cycle, a bad response can sail through unnoticed unless someone built a check for it — the code doesn't know the description it got back is subtly wrong, only that it got *a* response and moved on.

contentSections.scenario: A subscription box company's website used to auto-generate a friendly "welcome back" message for returning customers via an API call. This week, customers are reporting the message just says "Error: could not generate message" instead. Nothing about the website's code changed this week.
contentSections.question: Given nothing in the company's own code changed, what's the most likely cause?

options.label: The AI provider had an outage, changed something on their end, or the account's billing lapsed
Customers are typing something the AI can't understand
The website's internet connection is down

feedback.provider: Right. Since nothing on the company's side changed, the dependency that's still moving is the provider's side of the connection — an outage, a retired model version, or an expired payment method on the account are the usual suspects, and none of them are things the company's own code could have caused.
feedback.customer-input: Customers aren't typing anything into this feature at all — it's an automated welcome message triggered by their return visit, not something they compose. There's no customer input to blame here.
feedback.site-down: If the whole site's connection were down, nothing on the page would load at all, not just this one message. A single feature failing while the rest of the site works points elsewhere.

contentSections.mechanism: API calls create an ongoing dependency on a provider you don't control — outages, billing lapses and model retirements all show up exactly this way: a feature that worked yesterday fails today with nothing in your own code having changed.

contentSections.body: An API call is a request and a response over the internet, with the actual model living entirely on the provider's server — which is exactly why it costs money per use and can fail for reasons that have nothing to do with your own code.

contentSections.title: The dependency doesn't end at launch

contentSections.body: Six months after the shop owner's $400 description generator launches, she gets an email from the developer: "heads up — the provider is retiring the model version we built this on in 30 days, we'll need about an hour to move it to the newer one." Nothing broke. Nothing was her fault. It's just what an ongoing dependency on someone else's server means.

This is the piece that's easy to miss when "API" gets described as a one-time technical setup: it isn't. Every API-driven feature keeps depending, for as long as it runs, on the provider's server being up, the account's billing staying current, and the specific model version still being supported. None of that is a criticism of API calls as a pattern — it's simply what "the model lives on someone else's server" costs in exchange for not having to run that server yourself.

contentSections.question: Before moving on: if a provider announces a model version is being retired in 30 days, whose job is it to notice and act — the AI provider's, or the company that built the feature on top of it?
contentSections.answer: The company that built the feature. Providers typically give advance notice, but nothing forces the dependent feature to update itself — if nobody on the building side is watching for that notice, the feature simply breaks on the retirement date with no warning to its own users.
contentSections.hint: The provider's notice goes to whoever holds the API account — not to the feature's actual end users, who have no idea any of this exists.

contentSections.body: "We built the API integration" describes a launch, not a finish line — the dependency it creates keeps needing occasional attention for as long as the feature runs.

title: No-code and low-code AI tools, honestly assessed
description: What tools like Zapier, Make and built-in "AI steps" genuinely make possible without code — and the specific, real limits underneath the marketing, not a vague "it's more complicated."

learningObjectives.text: Name the concrete strengths of no-code AI tools for repetitive, well-defined tasks
Evaluate a no-code AI workflow for whether it's actually been tested against messy input

contentSections.body: A community garden coordinator spends a Saturday afternoon building an automation: a form for volunteers to report plant problems, wired through a no-code tool so that an AI drafts a helpful reply with care instructions, which gets emailed back automatically. She tests it with three tidy example reports. It works beautifully. She turns it on. By Tuesday, a volunteer has reported "the thing in the bed near the gate is dying, also is that a squash or a weed, hard to tell, sorry for the essay" — and the automation emails back three garbled sentences that don't answer either question.

contentSections.scenario: A colleague is deciding whether to trust a no-code AI workflow (built in a drag-and-drop tool with an AI step) with something that matters to the business.
contentSections.question: Which of these are genuine, real limits of no-code AI tools — not marketing complaints, but things that actually happen?

items.label: Messy or unexpected input is much harder to test for than a handful of tidy demo examples
When something goes wrong, there's often no way to see the exact request that was sent, only a vague error in a log
The platform's own per-run pricing stacks on top of the AI provider's per-request pricing as volume grows
No-code AI tools can't handle anything that matters — only toy projects
No-code workflows are always slower to run than custom code

explanation.edge-cases: This is the central honest limit — a demo tests the cases you thought of, and real users produce the cases you didn't.
explanation.debug-harder: Visual builders hide the raw request/response by design, for simplicity — which is great until something's wrong and you need to see exactly what was sent.
explanation.cost-scales: Most platforms meter runs above a free tier, and that's on top of whatever the AI provider itself bills — two separate costs compounding as usage grows.
explanation.no-real-use: Overstated — plenty of real, revenue-generating workflows run on no-code tools for years. The limit is about *which* tasks fit, not whether any do.
explanation.always-slower: Not generally true for the kind of simple, low-volume automation these tools are built for — the speed difference that matters is setup time, which usually favours no-code, not execution time.

contentSections.synthesis: No-code AI tools are genuinely useful and genuinely limited in specific, nameable ways — not vaguely "not as good as real code." The skill is knowing which limit applies to the task in front of you.

contentSections.body: The strengths are real too, and worth naming plainly: no engineer required, often working within an afternoon, connecting to dozens of existing tools (email, spreadsheets, Slack, CRMs) without anyone writing integration code, and cheap or free at low volume. For a huge share of small, repetitive tasks — routing form responses, drafting first replies, tagging incoming items — that's genuinely the right tool, not a compromise.

The honest assessment, then, isn't "no-code good" or "no-code bad" — it's that no-code tools shift where the risk sits. A custom-coded system puts the risk in whether the developer wrote it well. A no-code system puts the risk in whether *you* tested it against messy real input before trusting it, because the tool won't stop you from shipping something that only handles the happy path.
No-code AI tools genuinely earn their popularity for fast, low-volume, well-defined tasks — the failure mode to watch for is trusting a demo that only ever saw tidy input.

contentSections.title: Testing it like it's already broken

contentSections.body: The garden coordinator, after the squash-or-weed incident, does one thing differently before turning the automation back on: she deliberately feeds it the messiest, longest, most ambiguous volunteer report she can invent, on purpose, before trusting it with a real one.

contentSections.question: Put these into the order that actually stress-tests a no-code AI workflow before real use.
steps: Test with 2-3 clean, well-formed examples to confirm the basic wiring works
Deliberately test with a messy, unusually long, or ambiguous input
Check what the workflow does when a required field is completely blank
Turn the automation on for real traffic
contentSections.explanation: Clean examples confirm the wiring is connected correctly, but they can't tell you anything about resilience — that's what the deliberately messy and blank-field tests are for, and both need to happen before real traffic hits the workflow, not after something goes wrong.

contentSections.body: A no-code workflow that only ever met clean input hasn't been tested — it's been demonstrated.

title: When a script beats a conversation
description: The specific signal — repetition, fixed shape, no mid-task judgement needed — that tells you a chat prompt has outgrown chat, and the honest exception where it hasn't.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the three conditions under which scripting a repeated task pays off
Recognise when repetition alone doesn't justify automation because the judgement, not the format, is what repeats

contentSections.title: The eleventh time you type it

contentSections.body: Every Friday, a operations manager opens a chat window and types nearly the same 200-word prompt: "Here's this week's shift data [pastes table]. Reformat into our standard weekly summary: total hours by department, any overtime flagged, compare to last week." Ten weeks in, she's typed some version of that prompt ten times, pasted ten tables, and made the same three small corrections to the output each time because the AI keeps rounding overtime hours the same wrong way.

contentSections.scenario: The operations manager's weekly report task takes about 6 minutes of typing and correcting each time, in chat.
contentSections.question: If a script did this instead — same data source, same output format, automatically — roughly how many of those 6 minutes would still require her attention each week, once it's built and working?
contentSections.explanation: Once a script is built and tested against the recurring quirk (the overtime rounding), it should need zero minutes of her attention for a routine week — that's the entire point of moving a fixed, repeated task out of manual chat. The real cost isn't the ongoing minutes, it's the upfront time to build and test it, and the risk that a week's data doesn't fit the assumed shape and the script quietly produces something wrong with nobody watching.

contentSections.body: The signal that a script or automation beats a repeated conversation isn't "this task uses AI" — it's a specific combination: the task **repeats** on a schedule or trigger, the **shape of the output stays the same** each time, and a human doesn't need to steer or react mid-task. When all three hold, typing the same prompt by hand starts costing more than it needs to, in time and in the small inconsistencies that creep in when a tired person is doing the tenth near-identical thing that week.

The reverse also holds, and it's worth naming because "just automate everything repetitive" oversimplifies. A task can repeat and still be a bad fit for scripting if the *judgement* is the repeating part, not the format — deciding how to respond to an angry customer differs meaningfully case to case even though "respond to an angry customer" happens every week. Scripting that would mean encoding a fixed response pattern for something that genuinely needs a human reading each situation, which trades a small time cost for a real quality cost.
A repeated task is a candidate for scripting, not a guarantee — the real test is whether the *shape* repeats along with the frequency, or whether a human's judgement is what's actually recurring.

contentSections.title: The exception that keeps scripting honest

contentSections.body: A landlord automates rent reminder emails — same template, same trigger, works perfectly for eighteen months. He tries to do the same for tenant maintenance requests, feeding each one through a fixed script that auto-replies with a repair timeline. Two months in, a tenant's request ("the smell near the water heater is getting worse and now there's a stain on the ceiling below it") gets the same generic "we'll look at this within 5 business days" reply a squeaky-hinge request would get.

contentSections.scenario: The maintenance-request script treats a possible gas or water leak exactly the same as a squeaky hinge, because both arrived as a "maintenance request" and the script's job was to draft a timeline, not to judge urgency.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mismatch between this task and the scripting pattern?

options.label: The script's AI model isn't smart enough
The task looks repetitive (a maintenance request arrives) but the judgement inside it — how urgent, how serious — genuinely varies each time
Landlords shouldn't use AI for tenant communication at all

feedback.model: A more capable model could probably flag urgency better, but that's treating a design mismatch as a model-quality problem — the deeper issue is that the script was built to treat all requests the same, when they aren't.
feedback.judgement-varies: Right — this is the exception from lesson four's earlier point: repetition in *when* a task happens doesn't mean repetition in *what the right response is*. A water-heater leak and a squeaky hinge shouldn't get the same fixed-timeline reply.
feedback.never: The problem isn't AI in tenant communication generally — a well-built version could flag urgency and route serious issues to the landlord immediately. The problem is this specific script's design, treating every request as equally routine.

contentSections.mechanism: Whenever a script's fixed output doesn't vary but the situations feeding it genuinely do, the mismatch shows up as exactly this: technically-working automation producing quietly wrong responses.

contentSections.body: "This happens every week" is necessary for scripting to make sense, but not sufficient — check separately whether the right response also stays the same each time.

title: Choosing the simplest thing that works
description: Why the most sophisticated pattern is rarely the right one, and how to size the approach to the task's real volume and how much genuine judgement it needs.

learningObjectives.text: Match a task's volume and judgement needs to the simplest pattern that can do it reliably
Recognise over-engineering in both directions — too much automation, and too little for the volume

contentSections.body: A hobbyist baker wants to answer one recurring question from customers: "is this nut-free?" She reads a blog post about AI agents and spends a weekend building one — it's meant to check her ingredient database, cross-reference allergen rules, and reply to customer messages autonomously across three different platforms. It takes her two days to get working. It handles, on a good week, four questions. A simple pinned FAQ answer, or a one-line chat-drafted reply template she pastes in by hand, would have taken fifteen minutes and done the same job for four questions a week.

contentSections.intro: Build the decision for a real task: a freelance tutor wants to send a personalised weekly progress note to each of her 12 students' parents.

feedback.Once a year: Not this case — it's a recurring weekly task, which changes the calculation toward some automation.
feedback.Weekly, ongoing: Right — recurring and ongoing means the setup cost of automating has real weeks to pay itself back against.

feedback.12: Twelve is a small, human-manageable volume — not zero automation candidate, but nowhere near needing a multi-step autonomous system.
feedback.1,200: Not this case — she has 12 students, not 1,200.

fields.prompt: Does each note need real, individual judgement about that specific student's week, or is it a fixed template?

feedback.Real individual judgement each time: This is the key fact — she genuinely wants to say something true and specific about each student, not fill in a template.
feedback.Fully fixed template: Not quite — a tutoring progress note that reads the same for every student would lose the thing that makes it valuable to parents.

fields.prompt: Given weekly-but-small volume and real per-student judgement needed, what's the simplest thing that works?
options: A multi-step agent that reads each student's records and auto-sends notes with no review
A weekly chat session where she pastes her own notes on each student and asks for a polished draft, which she reviews before sending
fields.correctValue: A weekly chat session where she pastes her own notes on each student and asks for a polished draft, which she reviews before sending

feedback.A multi-step agent that reads each stude: This is more machinery than 12 notes a week justifies, and removes her review from something parents will read as personally observed — exactly the ingredient that makes the note worth sending.
feedback.A weekly chat session where she pastes h: Right-sized: low volume, genuine judgement needed, and a human review step preserved — chat is enough, and an agent would trade real signal (her own observations) for automation she doesn't need at this scale.

contentSections.synthesis: The simplest thing that works isn't about avoiding automation — it's matching the pattern's complexity to the task's actual volume and how much genuine judgement each instance needs. Twelve personal notes a week needing real judgement stays in chat; three hundred fixed-format confirmations a day moves to a pipeline.

contentSections.body: This is the practical thread that ties the whole module together. Chat, embedded features, API-driven scripts and agents form a rough ladder of increasing setup cost, increasing autonomy, and increasing difficulty to fully audit — and the honest rule is to climb it only as far as the task actually requires, never further because it sounds more impressive. Every rung above the one you need adds a failure mode without adding value: an agent doing a script's job can go wrong in more places than the script could; an API pipeline built for a task that happens twice a month mostly sits there costing maintenance attention for no real time saved.
Climb the ladder — chat, embedded feature, script, agent — only as far as the actual volume and complexity of the task requires, and treat every rung above that as cost, not sophistication.

Almost everyone who's tried building something with AI has one story like the nut-free-question agent — a tool built with more machinery than the job needed, because the machinery was interesting to build.

contentSections.question: Before answering for yourself: what's usually the real reason people over-build — pick the honest one, not the flattering one.
contentSections.answer: Most often it isn't that the task secretly needed the complexity — it's that the more sophisticated pattern was more interesting to build, or felt more impressive to show someone, than the two-minute version would have. That's a completely human reason, and naming it honestly is what makes it easier to catch next time.
contentSections.hint: Think about the last over-engineered thing you built or saw. Did the task need it, or did building it scratch a different itch?

contentSections.body: Describe the last time you built something more complicated than the task needed — what would the fifteen-minute version have looked like, and what did you actually get from building the bigger one instead?

title: Choose the right approach for seven ideas
description: Seven drills on the module's core skill: matching a task's actual volume, repetition and judgement needs to the simplest pattern that can do it.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the four-pattern distinction and the simplicity test at speed, across unfamiliar scenarios

contentSections.body: Nothing new here — seven drills across this module's skills: recognising the four patterns, assessing no-code tools honestly, deciding when scripting pays off, and sizing the approach to the task. Do them in one sitting or spread across a few — nothing here is timed.
If a drill needed a hint, that's worth noticing for the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Design an AI-powered tool on paper
description: Produce a one-page design — pattern, inputs, outputs, failure handling — for one real recurring task of your own, before building anything.

learningObjectives.text: Defend a chosen AI pattern against its neighbouring alternatives for a real task
Specify a tool's inputs, outputs and failure handling precisely enough for someone else to build from

contentSections.body: Every one of the tasks in this module — the shop's product descriptions, the tutor's progress notes, the charity's donor emails — started the same way: someone noticing a real, repeated task and deciding, on paper, what shape the AI part should take before building anything. This lab is that decision, made explicit, for a task of your own.

contentSections.title: Design an AI-powered tool — on paper, no code required
contentSections.brief: Pick one real, recurring task from your own work or life that currently costs you real time — something you'd genuinely want handled better. You are not building anything yet. You're producing the one-page design a developer, a no-code builder, or you yourself would work from, naming exactly what it needs to do and what happens when it doesn't.
contentSections.deliverable: A one-page design document naming: the chosen pattern (chat / script-API / agent / embedded feature) and why; the exact inputs the tool receives; the exact outputs it produces; and what happens at each of the three most likely ways it could fail.

stages.title: Pick the task and the pattern
stages.instructions: Describe the task in one paragraph: what triggers it, how often it happens, and what "done well" looks like. Then, using this module's tests (repetition, fixed shape, whether judgement varies, actual volume), name which of the four patterns fits — chat, script/API, agent, or embedded feature — and write two sentences defending that choice against the next rung up and the rung below it. If you genuinely can't defend it against a neighbouring rung, that's a sign to reconsider, not a step to skip.
stages.checkpoint: You have a task description, a chosen pattern, and a two-sentence defence against both neighbouring options.

stages.title: Specify inputs and outputs exactly
stages.instructions: Write down precisely what goes in (the exact data, text, or trigger — not "customer info," but which specific fields) and precisely what comes out (the exact shape of the output — a paragraph, a category label, a formatted email). Then write one sentence describing what "a good output" looks like specifically enough that someone else could judge it without asking you.
stages.checkpoint: Someone unfamiliar with the task could read your inputs and outputs and know exactly what data goes in and what should come out.

stages.title: Name the failure handling
stages.instructions: List the three most likely ways this could go wrong in real use — not "the AI could be wrong" in general, but specific failures (it produces the wrong format, it confidently states something false, the provider's service is unavailable, an input arrives that doesn't match what you expected). For each, write what actually happens: does a human see it before it goes out? Is there a fallback? How would you or a user even notice it happened?
stages.checkpoint: Each of the three failure modes has a named, concrete response — not "we'll deal with it if it happens."

rubric.criterion: Pattern choice is defended, not assumed
rubric.meets: The document explains why this pattern beats the two neighbouring rungs for this specific task's actual volume and judgement needs.

rubric.criterion: Inputs and outputs are exact
rubric.meets: A stranger could read the input/output spec and know precisely what data goes in and what shape comes out, with no follow-up questions.

rubric.criterion: Failure handling names real failures
rubric.meets: Three specific, plausible failure modes are named (not "it might not work"), each with a concrete human-in-the-loop or fallback response.

rubric.criterion: The task is real
rubric.meets: This is an actual recurring task from the author's own work or life, not a hypothetical example.

contentSections.body: A one-page design that names its own failure handling before a single line of code exists is worth more than a working prototype that's never been asked what happens when it's wrong.

contentSections.title: Checkpoint — Beyond the Chat Box

questions.from: This module — Chat, API, agent, embedded feature
questions.prompt: What actually distinguishes the four AI patterns from each other?

options.label: Who decides what to ask the model, and how often
How expensive each one is
Which one uses a "real" AI model

questions.explanation: All four use the same underlying models — the difference is entirely about who's deciding what gets asked, and how much a human is present for each individual exchange.

questions.from: This module — Chat, API, agent, embedded feature
questions.prompt: What's the defining trait of an embedded feature?

options.label: The user never sees a prompt or a chat window — someone else built the behaviour into a product in advance
It always costs more than an API call
It's the same thing as an agent, just simpler

questions.explanation: The recruiter's "Summarise this CV" button is the clearest example: no visible prompt, no conversation, behaviour fixed by whoever built the product.

questions.from: This module — What an API call actually is
questions.prompt: What actually happens when code "calls the API"?

options.label: A text request is sent over the internet to the provider's server, which sends back a text response
The AI model gets downloaded and installed locally
A chat window opens automatically for a human to use

questions.explanation: The model itself never leaves the provider's servers — it's a request and a response over the internet, the same shape as a web page loading.

questions.from: This module — What an API call actually is
questions.prompt: Why does an API-driven feature keep needing occasional attention after launch, unlike installed software?

options.label: It doesn't — once built, it's finished, same as an install
It depends on the provider's server, billing, and model version staying available and unchanged
Only because the internet occasionally goes down everywhere

questions.explanation: Providers retire model versions, have outages, and require current billing — none of which the company building on top of the API controls.

questions.from: This module — No-code and low-code AI tools, honestly assessed
questions.prompt: What's the real, specific limit of no-code AI tools, rather than the vague "they're not as good as real code"?

options.label: A demo tested with tidy examples doesn't reveal how the workflow handles messy, unexpected real input
No-code tools can't be used for anything that matters to a business
No-code workflows always run slower than coded ones

questions.explanation: The genuine risk is the gap between a convincing demo and real, messy traffic — not that the tools are inherently unsuited to real use.

questions.from: This module — No-code and low-code AI tools, honestly assessed
questions.prompt: What's a genuine strength of no-code AI tools?

options.label: No engineer required, connecting to many existing tools quickly, cheap at low volume
They never need testing
They can't fail once configured

questions.explanation: These are real, specific strengths — the trade is that testing against messy input is left entirely to the person building the workflow.

questions.from: This module — When a script beats a conversation
questions.prompt: What three conditions together suggest a repeated chat task should become a script?

options.label: The task repeats, the output's shape stays consistent, and no mid-task human judgement is needed
The task is done more than once, period
The AI got something wrong once

questions.explanation: Repetition alone isn't enough — the operations manager's weekly report and the tenant maintenance script show the difference a fixed shape and absent judgement make.

questions.from: This module — When a script beats a conversation
questions.prompt: Why did the tenant maintenance-request script go wrong, even though the task genuinely repeated?

options.label: The judgement (how urgent each request is) varied each time, even though the trigger repeated
The AI model was outdated
Landlords shouldn't automate tenant communication

questions.explanation: Repetition in when a task happens doesn't guarantee repetition in what the right response should be.

questions.from: This module — Choosing the simplest thing that works
questions.prompt: What's the practical rule for choosing among chat, embedded feature, script, and agent?

options.label: Climb the ladder only as far as the task's actual volume and judgement needs require
Always start with the most powerful option available
Agents are always the best choice for anything repeated

questions.explanation: Every rung above what the task needs adds a failure mode without adding value — the baker's nut-free-question agent is the clearest example.

questions.from: This module — Choosing the simplest thing that works
questions.prompt: "Over-engineered" in this module's sense can also describe what?

options.label: Too much manual effort applied to a volume that clearly needed automation, not only too much automation for a small task
Only ever too much automation, never too little
Any use of a script instead of chat

questions.explanation: The 40-person company hand-typing 300 confirmations a day is over-engineered in the opposite direction — too much manual effort for a volume that plainly needed a pipeline.

title: Finding the task worth automating
description: The actual test for whether a repetitive task deserves automation — a real trigger, real recurring cost, and a consistent shape — not just how annoying it feels.

learningObjectives.text: Identify a task's trigger, frequency and output consistency as the real basis for an automation decision
Estimate a task's real annual time cost before deciding whether automating it is worth the setup

contentSections.title: Not every annoying task is a candidate

contentSections.body: A nonprofit's grants coordinator complains constantly about a task that takes real time — reading each new funder's guidelines PDF and pulling out the deadline, the funding range, and eligibility rules into a shared tracker. She's also, separately, annoyed by a much smaller task: occasionally reformatting a chart when a board member asks for a different colour scheme. Both are annoying. Only one repeats predictably enough to be worth automating.

contentSections.scenario: Two tasks, both genuinely irritating to the grants coordinator: (A) reading a new funder PDF and logging three facts, which happens roughly 6 times a month, triggered by a new funder being added to a shared list; (B) reformatting a chart's colours, which happens rarely and only when a specific board member has a specific complaint that varies every time.
contentSections.question: Which is the stronger automation candidate, and on what basis?

options.label: A — it has a clear, repeating trigger and a consistent shape of output
B — it's more annoying, and annoyance is what matters most
Neither — automation only applies to tasks that use text generation

feedback.a: Right. Six times a month with a clear trigger (new funder added) and a consistent output shape (three specific facts into a tracker) is exactly the repeating, well-defined profile worth the setup effort.
feedback.b: Annoyance is what makes a task *feel* worth fixing, but it isn't what makes automation actually pay off — B happens rarely and varies every time, so there's little repetition to amortise any setup cost against.
feedback.neither: Automation candidates aren't limited to text generation — this module includes plenty of tasks (file sorting, data extraction, categorising) that use AI for one narrow judgement call inside an otherwise mechanical process.

contentSections.concept: A genuine automation candidate needs three things together: a **recognisable trigger** (something specific that starts it, not a vague feeling), **real recurring time cost** (not a one-off), and a **consistent output shape** each time — three facts into the same tracker fields, not "whatever the board member wants this time."

contentSections.body: This is worth separating from module one's scripting test, because it answers a different question. Module one asked "given a task, does it deserve a script or a conversation" — this asks something upstream of that: "out of everything I do repeatedly, which task is actually worth spending an afternoon automating at all?" A lot of repetitive tasks fail this test not because AI can't help, but because the *setup cost* would outweigh the *time actually saved* over a realistic horizon.

The honest arithmetic matters here: a task that takes 3 minutes, once a month, saves about 36 minutes a year if automated perfectly — probably less than the time spent building and testing the automation in the first place. A task that takes 10 minutes, every week, costs roughly 8.7 hours a year — a very different number, and one that starts to justify real setup time.

contentSections.scenario: A weekly task takes 12 minutes each time. It's been running, unautomated, for a year.
contentSections.question: Roughly how many hours has that task cost over the year?
contentSections.explanation: 12 minutes × 52 weeks = 624 minutes, or just over 10 hours a year — a number that's easy to underestimate when each individual instance feels small. This is the arithmetic worth doing honestly before dismissing a task as "too small to bother automating," and equally worth doing before over-investing in automating something that actually costs very little over a year.

contentSections.body: A task worth automating needs a real, recurring trigger and a consistent shape — annoyance alone doesn't pay for the setup, and a quiet arithmetic check (minutes × frequency) usually settles it faster than instinct does.

title: Wiring tools together without code
description: The trigger-then-actions skeleton every no-code automation shares, and where an AI step actually sits inside it.

learningObjectives.text: Describe the trigger/action structure common to no-code automation tools
Sequence a multi-step automation correctly based on which actions depend on earlier outputs

contentSections.title: One trigger, a chain of actions

contentSections.body: A dog groomer wants appointment confirmation texts to sound less like a robot and more like her — warm, a little informal, mentioning the dog's name. She's never touched a no-code tool before and pictures something like writing code. It isn't. It's closer to building with blocks: pick what starts it, then stack what happens next.

contentSections.question: Before the explanation: in a no-code automation, how many "triggers" does a single automation typically have — one, or can it react to several different starting events at once?
contentSections.answer: Almost always exactly one trigger per automation. If you want the same outcome to happen from two different starting events, you typically build two separate automations (or a trigger with two allowed variants of the same event, like "form submitted on form A or form B") rather than one automation with genuinely different triggers.
contentSections.hint: Think about what "trigger" means literally — the one thing that pulls it off the shelf and starts it running.

contentSections.body: The pattern is the same across every no-code tool, whatever it's called: one **trigger** (the event that starts things — a new form response, a scheduled time, an email arriving in a specific inbox) followed by a numbered sequence of **actions**. Each action typically takes the previous action's output as its input, which is why order matters: you can't send an AI-drafted welcome paragraph in an email before you've generated it, and you can't generate it before you know which workshop the trigger's form response named.

An AI step sits inside this exactly like any other action — it just happens to send its input to an AI provider's API instead of, say, a spreadsheet, and gets text back instead of a confirmation. That's the whole conceptual leap: nothing about wiring an AI step in is different from wiring in any other action, which is also why lesson three's real question — *where* in the chain that AI step belongs — matters more than how to technically connect it.
Every no-code automation reduces to the same shape: one trigger, then a numbered sequence of actions — an AI step is just one action among them, not a special category.

title: Where the AI step belongs in the chain
description: Why placement — not just presence — of the AI step determines whether an automation holds up, and how to separate deterministic checks from the part that genuinely needs judgement.

learningObjectives.text: Diagnose an automation failure caused by AI-step placement rather than AI quality
Design a chain that places deterministic checks before the AI step and human review after it where warranted

contentSections.title: First, or last, or in the middle

contentSections.body: A property manager's automation handles maintenance requests: tenant submits a form, AI drafts a reply with an estimated repair timeline, reply sends automatically. It runs fine for months. Then a tenant submits the same leaking-pipe report twice, five minutes apart, because the form didn't confirm submission clearly — and gets two replies with two different estimated timelines, because the AI's phrasing varies slightly each time it runs.

contentSections.scenario: The two-reply, two-different-estimates problem wasn't caused by the AI giving a wrong answer either time — both replies were individually reasonable. It was caused by something about where the AI step sat in the chain relative to other checks.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism behind this failure?

options.label: The AI model needs retraining to be more consistent

Nothing before the AI step checked whether this was a duplicate submission, so the AI step ran twice on the same underlying issue and (reasonably) produced two slightly different, individually-fine answers
AI should never estimate timelines

feedback.retrain: The AI's individual answers were each reasonable — the problem isn't answer quality, it's that the same underlying request reached the AI step twice with nothing catching that duplication first.
feedback.no-dedupe: Right. This is a placement problem, not an AI-quality problem: a duplicate-check is a simple, deterministic step that belongs before the AI step, filtering out the second submission before it ever reaches judgement.
feedback.never-estimate: AI estimating a repair timeline from a description is a reasonable use of judgement — the issue is a missing check earlier in the chain, not the estimation task itself.

contentSections.mechanism: Placement failures like this show up as "the AI gave two different answers," but the real cause is upstream — a deterministic check that should have filtered the case before it reached the judgement-requiring step never existed.

contentSections.body: The general rule: put **deterministic, rule-based checks** — is this a duplicate, is required data present, does this even qualify — *before* the AI step, so the AI step only ever handles the part that genuinely needs judgement. Put **human review**, when it's needed, *after* the AI step, for the same reason lesson three of module one raised: an AI step producing something that lands emotionally or financially (a rejection letter, a refund decision) usually needs a checkpoint before it goes out, not blind trust that the first draft is the final answer.

This also answers a question worth asking of every automation: what is the *smallest* part of this chain that actually needs AI? In the maintenance request example, checking for duplicates doesn't need AI at all — a simple rule (same tenant, same unit, same category, within 30 minutes) handles it. Estimating a repair timeline from a free-text description genuinely benefits from AI's ability to read varied phrasing. Putting AI only where the judgement is needed, and plain rules everywhere else, is what makes the whole chain both cheaper to run and easier to reason about when something goes wrong.

contentSections.intro: Design the chain for: a landlord wants tenant maintenance requests triaged by urgency, with genuinely urgent ones (leaks, no heat, no working lock) flagged to him immediately, and routine ones getting an AI-drafted acknowledgment with an estimated timeline.

fields.prompt: What should the very first step after the trigger be?
options: The AI step, drafting a reply immediately
A duplicate check, filtering out repeat submissions of the same issue
fields.correctValue: A duplicate check, filtering out repeat submissions of the same issue

feedback.The AI step, drafting a reply immediatel: This risks the same double-reply problem from the hook — nothing filters duplicates before judgement runs.
feedback.A duplicate check, filtering out repeat: Right — a simple rule-based filter belongs first, before anything judgement-requiring runs.

fields.prompt: Where should urgency triage happen — is "leak / no heat / no lock" a job for AI judgement or a simple rule?
options: A simple rule matching against a short list of urgent keywords/categories
An AI step reading the whole description and deciding urgency each time
fields.correctValue: A simple rule matching against a short list of urgent keywords/categories

feedback.A simple rule matching against a short l: Right for the clear-cut cases — a fixed list of urgent categories is deterministic and doesn't need AI's judgement at all, which also makes it faster and easier to trust.
feedback.An AI step reading the whole description: This works but is heavier than the task needs for the clear-cut urgent categories — reserve AI judgement for descriptions that don't match an obvious category.

fields.prompt: Where does the AI step actually belong in this chain?
options: Drafting the acknowledgment/timeline reply, only for requests the rule-based triage already marked routine
fields.correctValue: Drafting the acknowledgment/timeline reply, only for requests the rule-based triage already marked routine

feedback.Drafting the acknowledgment/timeline rep: Right — the AI step handles exactly the part that needs judgement (a natural-sounding, specific-feeling reply), after the deterministic steps have already filtered and triaged.
feedback.First, before any triage happens: This is the placement mistake the whole lesson is about — urgent requests would get a routine AI-drafted acknowledgment instead of an immediate flag to the landlord.

contentSections.synthesis: The chain that holds up: duplicate check → rule-based urgency triage → (urgent: immediate flag to landlord, bypassing AI entirely) → (routine: AI-drafted acknowledgment). AI sits exactly where judgement is genuinely needed, with deterministic rules doing everything else.

contentSections.body: Put simple, rule-based checks before the AI step so it only ever sees what genuinely needs judgement — and put human review after it when the output carries real weight.

title: What happens when a step fails
description: Why silent failure, not occasional errors, is the actual risk — and the three questions (what happens instead, who finds out, how you'd notice a pattern) that turn a fragile chain into one you can trust.

learningObjectives.text: Diagnose a silent-failure automation design and name what's missing
Design failure handling that names a fallback, a notification path, and a deliberate test

contentSections.title: Silent failure is the dangerous kind

contentSections.body: A community theatre's ticket-confirmation automation quietly stops sending confirmations for exactly one show, because that show's title contains an apostrophe that breaks the AI step's request formatting. Nobody notices — not the theatre, not the automation, not the sixty people who never got their confirmation — until opening night, when a line of confused ticket-holders forms at the door.

contentSections.code: Automation design notes: "Trigger: new ticket purchase. Action 1: send purchase details to AI, get a personalised confirmation message. Action 2: email that message to the buyer. (No other steps.)"
contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw in this design, given the apostrophe incident?

options.text: There's no fallback or notification for when action 1 fails to produce a usable message
The AI step shouldn't be used for confirmation messages at all

feedback.no-fallback: Right. Nothing in this design says what happens if action 1 fails or produces something malformed — the whole chain just quietly doesn't complete, and nobody is told.
feedback.no-ai: AI drafting a personalised confirmation isn't the problem — the problem is that the design has no answer for what happens when that step doesn't work as expected.
feedback.wrong-order: The order is fine — you need the confirmation message before you can email it. The missing piece is what happens when generating that message fails, not the sequence itself.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A two-action chain with no failure handling has exactly one path: success. Any failure — a formatting error, a timeout, an unexpected character in the input — has nowhere to go except silently dropping the whole ticket confirmation, which is precisely what happened.

contentSections.body: Real failure handling doesn't need to be elaborate. At minimum, it means answering three questions for every step that could fail: **what happens instead of the intended action** (retry once, send a plain fallback message, skip and log it); **who or what finds out** (an email digest, a flagged row in a spreadsheet, a notification); and **how you'd know if it were happening a lot**, not just once. A fallback plain-text confirmation — "Thanks for your purchase! We'll follow up with details shortly" — sent whenever the AI step fails, plus a log entry, would have caught the apostrophe problem within a day instead of a month.
An automation with no failure handling has exactly one path — success — and everything else vanishes silently until its real-world consequence shows up somewhere else.

title: Automations that don't need babysitting
description: The difference between an automation you trust and one you're still manually supervising every day — and the specific, checkable signals that earn the difference.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish genuine automation trust from daily manual re-checking
Identify concrete mechanisms (failure notifications, spot-checks, a demonstrated track record) that reduce the need for constant supervision

contentSections.body: Six months after building an invoice-extraction automation, a bookkeeper still opens the results spreadsheet every single morning and reads every row, just in case. Her business partner asks why. "Because what if it's wrong and I don't catch it." That's not an unreasonable worry — but it also means the automation has saved her zero minutes of daily attention, even though it's saved her the typing.

contentSections.scenario: The bookkeeper wants to know which of these would actually let her stop daily checking, versus which would just make her feel better without changing anything real.
contentSections.question: Which of these genuinely reduce the need for daily babysitting?

items.label: A notification that only fires when a row fails or looks malformed, instead of a full spreadsheet to re-read daily
A scheduled weekly spot-check of a random sample, instead of reading every row every day
A track record of two straight weeks with the failure handling from lesson four catching every deliberately-triggered failure
Simply deciding to trust it more after enough time has passed, without changing anything about how it's monitored
Switching to a more expensive or capable AI model

explanation.notify-on-fail: This directly replaces daily full review with attention only when something's actually wrong — the core move from babysitting to trust.
explanation.weekly-spotcheck: A scheduled, spaced spot-check catches drift over time without requiring daily attention — this is what "trust but verify" looks like in practice.
explanation.track-record: A demonstrated record against deliberately-triggered failures (from lesson four's test step) is real evidence the handling works, not just a hope that it does.
explanation.just-time: Time alone changes nothing about whether the automation is actually reliable — this is exactly the false confidence that keeps someone checking daily out of habit rather than reasoned trust.
explanation.bigger-model: A more capable model might reduce errors somewhat, but it doesn't address the actual gap here, which is the absence of any signal that tells her when something's wrong.

contentSections.synthesis: Moving from daily babysitting to genuine automation isn't about the AI getting better — it's about building specific, checkable signals (failure notifications, spaced spot-checks, a demonstrated track record) that make trust earned rather than assumed.

contentSections.body: This closes the loop the whole module has been building: lesson one found a real candidate task, lesson two wired it, lesson three placed the AI step correctly, lesson four gave it failure handling — and lesson five is the honest test of whether all of that actually adds up to something you can stop watching. If you still need to check it every day, something upstream — usually the failure handling — isn't actually doing its job yet.
The real sign an automation is working isn't that it never fails — it's that you'd actually know if it did, without having to check every day to find out.

title: Design seven automations with failure handling
description: Seven drills on this module's core skills: candidate selection, chain wiring, AI-step placement, and failure handling that's actually been tested.

learningObjectives.text: Apply candidate selection, chain design, AI-step placement and failure handling at speed across unfamiliar scenarios

contentSections.body: Seven drills across this module's skills: spotting a real automation candidate, wiring the chain, placing the AI step correctly, and building in failure handling that's actually been tested. Nothing here is timed.
If a drill needed a hint, that's worth watching for in the checkpoint, not a reason to redo the set.

title: Build one automation you'll actually use
description: Build, deliberately test the failure handling of, and run for two real weeks one automation of your own — with an honest record of whether it actually stuck.

learningObjectives.text: Build a working automation with the AI step correctly placed and its failure handling deliberately tested
Evaluate, from two weeks of real use, whether the automation is worth keeping

contentSections.body: Every lesson in this module has been building toward one thing: an automation that actually survives contact with your real, messy week — not a demo that worked once. This lab builds one, and then checks whether it holds up over two real weeks, not just a first test run.

contentSections.title: Build one automation you'll actually use
contentSections.brief: Using the task you identified in module one's lab, or a new one that passes lesson one's test (real trigger, real recurring cost, consistent shape), build one working automation — in whatever no-code tool, script, or even a disciplined manual routine with an AI step you have access to. Then run it for two weeks against real, live use, and record honestly whether you kept using it.
contentSections.deliverable: A working automation, described precisely (trigger, actions, where the AI step sits, its failure handling), plus a two-week log: did it run, did anything fail, did you keep using it or abandon it, and why.

stages.title: Confirm the candidate and design the chain
stages.instructions: Restate the task, its trigger, and its consistent shape. Sketch the full chain: trigger, then each action in order, marking clearly which steps are deterministic checks and which step is the AI step, using lesson three's placement principle.
stages.checkpoint: You have a written chain with the AI step placed after any deterministic filtering it depends on.

stages.title: Add real failure handling
stages.instructions: For the AI step and any other step that could fail, name what happens instead (retry, fallback, flag to a human), how you'd be notified, and — critically — actually trigger each failure type once on purpose (a malformed input, a missing field, whatever you can deliberately break) to confirm the handling fires as designed.
stages.checkpoint: Each failure mode has been deliberately triggered at least once and the handling was observed to work, not just assumed to.

stages.title: Run it live
stages.instructions: Turn it on for real use. Let it run against actual, live triggers for two weeks, checking in no more than the frequency you'd genuinely be willing to sustain long-term (per lesson five — not daily out of anxiety).
stages.checkpoint: The automation has run against real triggers, not just test data, for the full two weeks.

stages.title: Write the honest two-week record
stages.instructions: Record: how many times it ran, whether anything failed and what the failure handling did about it, whether you actually kept using it or quietly went back to doing the task manually, and if you abandoned it, the real reason why — not a flattering one.
stages.checkpoint: The record states plainly whether the automation is still in use, with a specific, honest reason either way.

rubric.criterion: The task genuinely passes lesson one's test
rubric.meets: A real trigger, real recurring cost, and consistent shape are all named specifically, not asserted vaguely.

rubric.criterion: The AI step is placed correctly
rubric.meets: Deterministic checks sit before the AI step; the AI step handles only the part that needs genuine judgement.

rubric.criterion: Failure handling was actually tested
rubric.meets: At least one failure type was deliberately triggered and the response was observed, not just designed on paper.

rubric.criterion: The two-week record is honest
rubric.meets: States plainly whether the automation is still in use after two real weeks, with a specific reason — including if the honest answer is that it was abandoned.

contentSections.body: An automation that survives two real weeks and gets an honest verdict is worth more than a demo that worked once and was never checked on again.
