title: Tokens and how usage is billed
description: The actual unit AI providers bill by — tokens, counted on both input and output — and why that makes length, not "a use," the real cost driver.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what a token is and why both input and output are billed
Estimate roughly how many tokens a given piece of text represents

contentSections.body: A small marketing agency's account manager gets a monthly invoice from their AI provider: $187.42. Not $187, not $190 — a number with cents, like an electricity bill. She'd assumed, reasonably, that "we pay for AI" meant something closer to a flat monthly fee like their design software subscription. It doesn't. It's metered, the same way electricity is — you get charged for exactly how much you used, down to fractions of a cent per request.

contentSections.question: Before the explanation: what do you think is actually being measured and charged for, on a per-request basis — is it the number of requests, the number of words, or something else?
contentSections.answer: It's neither requests nor whole words — it's tokens, small chunks of text (roughly 4 characters, or about three-quarters of a word, for English). A request with a 500-word input and a 100-word response is billed on something close to the token count of both combined, not on "one request" as a flat unit.
contentSections.hint: If billing were purely per-request, a one-word question and a 10-page document would cost the same to process. They don't.

contentSections.body: A **token** is the actual unit AI providers bill by — a small chunk of text, roughly four characters or three-quarters of a word in English ("summarise" might be one or two tokens; "the" is one; a rare or unusual word might be split into several). Every request has an **input** token count (what you send — instructions plus any content) and an **output** token count (what comes back), and providers typically price these two differently, with output usually costing more per token than input, because generating new text takes more computation than reading existing text.

This is the mechanical reason length drives cost so directly. A one-line question costs almost nothing — maybe a few hundred tokens total. Summarising a 20-page report might involve tens of thousands of input tokens alone. Neither request is a flat "one use" — the bill scales with how much text moved through the system, in both directions, which is exactly why the hobbyist's 200-article weekend added up to real money even though each individual summary felt small.

contentSections.scenario: A typical paragraph of English text — about 5 sentences, roughly 100 words.
contentSections.question: Roughly how many tokens is that?
contentSections.explanation: About 130 tokens is a reasonable estimate for 100 words of ordinary English — the rule of thumb (roughly 0.75 words per token, or equivalently about 1.3 tokens per word) holds up well for everyday prose, though it shifts for text with unusual words, code, or non-English languages, which often tokenize less efficiently.

contentSections.body: AI usage is billed like a meter, not a subscription: by tokens — small chunks of text — counted on both what you send in and what comes back, which is why length drives cost directly.

title: Estimating the cost of a workflow before you build it
description: The actual arithmetic — volume × tokens × price, for input and output separately — and why running it before launch catches costs that only show up at scale.

learningObjectives.text: Calculate an estimated monthly cost for a workflow given volume, token estimates and pricing
Distinguish an honestly-labelled estimate from false precision

contentSections.title: Do the arithmetic before, not after

contentSections.body: A wedding photographer builds an automation drafting personalised thank-you notes to every couple after their gallery delivery — cheap and lovely at her current 15 weddings a year. A blog post about her workflow goes semi-viral in a photography Facebook group; forty other photographers copy her exact setup, several running it against client lists of 300+. None of them ran the arithmetic first, because at 15 weddings a year the cost was small enough to never think about.

Estimating cost before building isn't complicated arithmetic — it's the same shape every time: **(volume) × (average input tokens per use) × (input price)**, plus **(volume) × (average output tokens per use) × (output price)**. The two halves get calculated separately because input and output are almost always priced differently, then added together. Doing this before building, using module two's own habit of designing before wiring anything, catches the cases where a workflow that felt free at 15 uses a year turns out to cost real money at 300.

The honest caveat: an estimate is only as good as its volume and length assumptions, and both are genuinely hard to know in advance for a brand-new workflow. The useful habit isn't demanding perfect numbers — it's running the calculation with your best honest guess, labelling which parts are guesses, and re-running it once real usage data exists. A rough estimate done before launch beats an exact number discovered on the first invoice.

contentSections.scenario: The wedding photographer's thank-you note automation costs about $0.02 per use at her original volume of 15 weddings a year.
contentSections.question: If the exact same per-use cost held at the 300-client-list volume several copycats were running, roughly what would the annual cost be?
contentSections.explanation: $0.02 × 300 = $6 a year — genuinely still small. The real risk in the hook wasn't that the per-use cost was secretly huge; it's that nobody had checked whether it was small, and a workflow that scales past 300 into the thousands, or uses a pricier model, or generates longer output, stops being obviously fine the moment nobody's done the arithmetic.

contentSections.body: Cost estimation is volume × tokens-in × input price, plus volume × tokens-out × output price — done before building, with honestly-labelled guesses where exact numbers aren't yet known.

title: Subscriptions versus usage billing
description: Why a consumer chat subscription and API usage billing aren't the same product priced differently — they fit different usage patterns, and mismatching them is what usually causes the surprise.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish what a chat subscription grants access to from what an automation actually needs
Evaluate whether a subscription or usage billing fits a given usage pattern

contentSections.title: Two different products, not two prices for the same thing

contentSections.body: A freelance writer pays $20/month for a chat subscription she uses daily, for hours, drafting and revising client work. A separate small e-commerce shop pays roughly $6 a month in usage billing for an automation that occasionally drafts a product description. Both are "using AI." Neither would be well served by swapping to the other's billing model.

contentSections.scenario: The writer tries switching to usage billing to "save money," since she'd heard it's often cheaper. Her first month's usage bill comes to $47 — more than double her old subscription.
contentSections.question: What actually happened?

options.label: Usage billing rates went up unexpectedly that month
Her usage pattern — hours of daily, steady chatting — is exactly the profile a flat subscription is priced to cover cheaply; the same volume under a per-token meter adds up fast
She was charged twice by mistake

feedback.rates-up: Nothing in the scenario suggests a rate change — the more likely, and more instructive, explanation is about her usage pattern itself, not a pricing anomaly.
feedback.pattern-mismatch: Right. Subscriptions are priced as a bet that heavy, steady users will use more than $20 worth of usage-billed tokens — which is exactly her profile. The provider isn't losing money on subscribers like her; that's who the flat fee is designed around.
feedback.double-charge: There's no indication of a billing error here — the number is consistent with her actual, heavy, steady usage simply costing more per-token than a flat monthly fee.

contentSections.mechanism: A subscription's flat price is a bet, by the provider, about typical usage — heavy, steady users cost the provider more in actual compute than $20 buys under a per-token meter, and the flat fee exists partly because it's simpler and partly because enough light users balance out the heavy ones. Switching a heavy, steady usage pattern to per-token billing removes that balancing.

contentSections.body: The practical rule: a **subscription** suits an individual with steady, high-frequency use of a chat interface, where a flat fee is predictable and often cheaper than metering it. **Usage billing** suits automations, variable workloads, and anything code-driven, where volume genuinely varies month to month and a fixed fee would either be wasted or insufficient. They aren't two prices for the same product — they're priced for two different usage shapes, and the mismatch, not the price itself, is usually what causes a nasty surprise.

Subscriptions and usage billing aren't cheap-versus-expensive — they're priced for different usage shapes, and picking the one that matches your actual pattern matters more than picking the one that sounds cheaper.

title: Cheap models for cheap steps
description: Why paying premium per-token prices for every step of a workflow wastes money on tasks that don't need it — and how to judge which steps genuinely do.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate whether a workflow step's difficulty justifies a more capable, pricier model
Match model choice to task complexity rather than defaulting to the most capable option everywhere

contentSections.title: Match the model to the judgement, not the budget

contentSections.body: A small law firm runs two AI-driven tasks: (1) flagging which incoming emails are new client inquiries versus existing-client admin, a simple two-way split, and (2) drafting first-pass arguments for a genuinely complex, multi-issue contract dispute. They use the same top-tier, most expensive model for both — mostly because nobody thought to ask whether the email-flagging task needed it.

contentSections.code: Team decision: "We'll standardise on one model across all our AI features, to keep things simple — our most capable one, since it's the safest choice for everything."
contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw in "use the most capable model for everything, to be safe"?

options.text: It pays premium per-token pricing on simple tasks that a cheaper model would likely handle just as reliably, without any real safety benefit
Cheaper models are never safe to use for anything
Using different models for different tasks is technically impossible

feedback.overpay: Right. "Safest" here is doing very little real work — a simple two-way email split isn't meaningfully safer with a top-tier model, but it is meaningfully more expensive, especially at real volume.
feedback.never-safe: The flaw isn't that cheaper models are unsafe — plenty of narrow, well-defined tasks are exactly what they're built for. The flaw is applying one model to every task regardless of what that task actually needs.
feedback.impossible: Using different models for different steps within the same system is a completely normal, common pattern — nothing technical prevents it.

contentSections.flawExplanation: "Standardise for simplicity" sounds sensible but conflates operational simplicity with cost-effectiveness — the actual fix is matching model capability (and price) to each task's real difficulty, the same discipline module one applied to choosing chat vs. script vs. agent.

contentSections.body: The judgement to make, per task, is roughly: does this step require synthesising a lot of context, reasoning through several dependent steps, or producing genuinely nuanced or creative writing? If yes, the more capable (and pricier) model likely earns its cost. If the task is narrow — classify, extract, format, apply a simple fixed rule — a cheaper, faster model is very likely to do it just as reliably, for a fraction of the per-token price, and often faster too.
Match a model's cost to a step's actual difficulty, not to the whole system's most demanding task — a cheap model on a simple classification step isn't a compromise, it's the correct choice.

title: Free tiers, limits and what happens at the wall
description: The three genuinely different ways a free tier can run out — a rate limit, expired trial credit, or a monthly cap — and why planning for the specific one that applies beats discovering it mid-project.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish rate limits, trial credit expiry and monthly caps as different kinds of free-tier limit
Plan a fallback for a free-tier limit before a project depends on it

contentSections.title: The wall isn't always the same wall

contentSections.body: A retiree building a small hobby tool for his local chess club's tournament pairings hits, over three months, three completely different free-tier walls at three different providers he tried: one just stopped responding for an hour (a rate limit), one asked for a credit card to continue (expired trial credit), and one quietly reset on the first of the month with no warning at all (a monthly cap). He'd assumed "free tier ran out" meant one thing. It meant three.

Free tiers exist to let people try a product cheaply, and providers structure the limit differently depending on what they're protecting against: a **rate limit** protects their servers from being overwhelmed in a short burst (usually resolves itself — wait a minute, try again); a fixed **credit allowance** is a one-time trial amount that, once spent, needs a paid account to continue; a recurring **monthly cap** resets on a schedule and is meant for genuinely light, ongoing use. None of these is "the AI stopped working" — each is a specific, checkable limit with its own specific next step.

A free tier's wall isn't one thing — checking which kind of limit you're up against (rate, trial credit, or monthly cap) is what tells you whether to wait a minute, add a payment method, or wait for next month.

title: Cost one of your own workflows at scale
description: Build a stated-assumptions cost model for a real workflow at 100 and 10,000 uses, and check it against subscription and free-tier alternatives.

learningObjectives.text: Calculate a workflow's cost at two different scales with explicit, honestly-labelled assumptions
Evaluate whether usage billing, a subscription, or a free tier best fits a workflow at a given scale

contentSections.body: Every estimate in this module has used made-up numbers for a made-up workflow. This lab uses your own — a real workflow, real assumptions, stated honestly, projected out to a scale that would actually matter if it were true.

contentSections.title: Cost one of your own workflows at scale
contentSections.brief: Take a real workflow — one you built in this phase's earlier labs, or a real one you use or are considering. Build a cost model for it at two very different scales: 100 uses, and 10,000 uses. State every assumption plainly, especially the ones you're least sure of.
contentSections.deliverable: A cost model document showing the calculation and result at 100 uses and at 10,000 uses, with every assumption (token estimates, model choice, pricing source) stated explicitly, including which numbers are confident and which are honest guesses.

stages.title: Establish your per-use numbers
stages.instructions: Name the workflow and estimate, per single use: average input tokens and average output tokens. If you don't have exact numbers, estimate honestly from a real example (using lesson one's ~0.75-words-per-token rule of thumb) and label it as an estimate. Choose a model tier (lesson four) and state why it fits the task's actual difficulty.
stages.checkpoint: You have a stated per-use input and output token estimate, a chosen model tier, and a one-sentence justification for that model choice.

stages.title: Build the model at 100 and 10,000 uses
stages.instructions: Using lesson two's formula (volume × tokens × price, for input and output separately, added together), calculate total cost at 100 uses and again at 10,000 uses. Show the arithmetic, not just the final numbers — someone else should be able to follow exactly how you got there.
stages.checkpoint: Both scale calculations are shown with visible arithmetic, not just final totals.

stages.title: Sanity-check against the alternatives
stages.instructions: At each scale, note whether a subscription (lesson three) would make more or less sense than usage billing, and whether a free tier (lesson five) could plausibly cover the 100-use scenario, the 10,000-use scenario, both, or neither — and if a free tier's limits would be hit, name which kind (rate, credit, or cap).
stages.checkpoint: The document states, for both scales, whether usage billing, a subscription, or a free tier is the sounder fit, with a one-sentence reason.

rubric.criterion: Assumptions are stated, not hidden
rubric.meets: Every input to the calculation (token estimates, pricing, volume) is named explicitly, with genuine guesses labelled as such.

rubric.criterion: The arithmetic is shown and correct
rubric.meets: Both the 100-use and 10,000-use totals are calculated using volume × tokens × price for input and output separately, with visible working.

rubric.criterion: Model choice is justified by task difficulty
rubric.meets: The chosen model tier is defended against the task's actual complexity, not assumed to be the most capable available option.

rubric.criterion: The billing-model comparison is real
rubric.meets: Subscription, usage billing and free-tier fit are each addressed at both scales with a concrete reason, not a generic statement.

contentSections.body: A cost model that's honest about its own uncertain assumptions is more useful than a confident number nobody can trace back to a real calculation.

title: A prompt library for the things you do repeatedly
description: Why a saved, refined prompt for a genuinely repeated task beats reconstructing it from memory each time — and the lightweight test for what's worth saving.

learningObjectives.text: Recognise when inconsistent AI results come from prompt variation rather than the model itself
Identify which repeated tasks are worth a saved library entry

contentSections.body: A high school teacher asks an AI tool to help turn her rough lesson notes into a structured outline, most weeks, for whichever subject she's prepping next. She's never saved the prompt anywhere — she retypes something close to it from memory each time, and about one week in four, the result comes back oddly generic, because that week she forgot to mention the specific grade level, or forgot to ask for discussion questions at the end.

contentSections.scenario: Two colleagues both use AI to help draft meeting agendas. One has a prompt saved in a notes app — exact wording, refined over three uses until it consistently produces the format her team likes — that she copies and reuses. The other retypes a similar request from scratch each time, phrasing it a little differently depending on how rushed she is.
contentSections.question: Which one is actually building a personal AI system, in the sense this module means it?

options.label: The one with the saved, reused prompt
The one retyping it fresh each time — that shows more skill with the tool
Neither — a real system requires automation, like module two's

feedback.saved: Right. A personal AI system doesn't require code or automation — it can be as simple as a prompt, refined once, saved somewhere, and reused deliberately instead of reconstructed from memory.
feedback.fresh: Retyping from scratch each time isn't a sign of skill — it's the reason results vary, since small unintentional wording differences change the output. The saved version is the more deliberate, more skilled approach.
feedback.neither: Module two's automations remove a human from the loop entirely; this module is about something lighter-weight — prompts and templates a human still actively uses, on purpose, saved rather than reinvented.

contentSections.concept: A **prompt library entry** is a saved, deliberately refined prompt for a task you actually repeat — not automated, still used by hand each time, but no longer reconstructed from memory with all the small, accidental variation that produces.

contentSections.body: This sits one rung below module two's automations on the same ladder from module one: automation removes you from a repeated task entirely; a saved prompt keeps you fully in the loop, choosing when to use it, but stops you from having to reinvent the wording every single time. Not every repeated task deserves full automation — some just deserve a good prompt, written once and kept.

The test for whether something belongs in a library is close to module two's automation-candidate test, but lighter: does this come up regularly enough, in a similar enough shape, that a saved version would consistently save real effort — even if it's used by hand, a few times a week, forever? A one-off, highly specific request doesn't pass that test even if it was a great prompt in the moment; it simply won't recur in that shape.
A prompt library entry is any saved, refined prompt for something you genuinely repeat — the point isn't automating it away, it's never having to reconstruct good wording from memory again.

title: Templates for your recurring tasks
description: Turning a saved prompt into a real template by explicitly naming every variable slot, instead of leaving any of it to memory.

learningObjectives.text: Convert a saved prompt into a template with explicit, clearly marked variable slots
Test a template's completeness by checking whether it depends on unstated memory

contentSections.body: A freelance grant writer has a saved prompt for turning a client's rough notes into a polished paragraph. It works well — except she still has to remember, every time, to mention which funder's style guidelines apply, because the saved prompt never actually asks for that. Two months in, she realises she's saved a prompt that still depends on her memory for the one detail that changes most.

contentSections.problem: Turn a working prompt ("Turn these rough notes into a polished grant paragraph") into a proper template.

steps.label: Identify what actually varies between uses
steps.work: The rough notes themselves, the specific funder's style guidelines, and the target paragraph length all change every time. The overall task — "turn notes into a polished paragraph" — stays the same.
steps.why: You can't mark variable slots until you've actually named everything that changes, not just the most obvious one.

steps.label: Write the fixed wording with explicit slots
steps.work: "Turn these rough notes into a polished grant paragraph: [NOTES]. Match the style guidelines for [FUNDER]. Target length: [WORD COUNT]."
steps.why: Every changing part now has its own clearly marked slot — nothing is left for memory to supply.

steps.label: Test it as if you were someone else
steps.work: She reads the template as if she'd never written it: is it obvious what [FUNDER] means and what to put there? Yes — reasonably self-explanatory. Is [NOTES] clear? Yes. The template holds up.
steps.why: A template only proves itself once it's been read by someone (even a future, forgetful version of yourself) who didn't write it.

faded.problem: Same idea, for a different recurring task: drafting a LinkedIn post from a rough idea, matching a specific tone and including a call to action.

blanks.prompt: What varies between uses of this LinkedIn-post prompt?
blanks.answer: the rough idea, the desired tone, and the specific call to action
accept: the idea, the tone, and the CTA
rough idea, tone, call to action
blanks.why: Naming all three, not just the most obvious one (the idea), is what prevents the template from silently depending on memory for the other two.

blanks.prompt: Write the templated version with explicit slots.
blanks.answer: Turn this rough idea into a LinkedIn post: [IDEA]. Tone: [TONE]. End with a call to action: [CTA].
accept: Draft a LinkedIn post from [IDEA] in [TONE] tone, ending with [CTA]
blanks.why: Each changing element gets its own visible slot, so using the template correctly doesn't require remembering what usually goes there.

faded.procedure: List every part of the request that changes between uses, however minor it seems, then give each one its own explicit, clearly labelled slot in the wording — nothing implied, nothing left to memory.

contentSections.body: The test worth applying to any template before trusting it: would it still work correctly if you hadn't used it in six months and had genuinely forgotten the context? If the answer depends on remembering something the template itself doesn't say, that's an unmarked variable slot hiding inside what looks like a finished template.
A template's whole job is naming every changing part explicitly — anything left implied is a variable slot quietly depending on memory, which is exactly the problem a template exists to remove.

title: Routines for a low-capacity day
description: Building a pre-decided, minimal-decision version of a library entry for the days when even small choices cost more than usual.

learningObjectives.text: Recognise why open decisions in a template become costlier on a low-capacity day
Convert a full template into a low-capacity version by pre-deciding its open choices

contentSections.title: The version with nothing left to decide

contentSections.body: A parent managing a chronic health condition has a beautifully templated library entry for drafting emails to her kids' school — tone, formality, and specific points all left as blanks to fill thoughtfully. On a genuinely bad day, she opens it, stares at the three blanks, and closes the tab. Not because the template is bad — because on that day, deciding tone and formality is exactly the kind of small cost she doesn't have to spend.

This is the module's most direct application of the same idea behind a bad-day path anywhere else: not every version of a tool needs to ask the same amount of you. A **low-capacity library entry** takes a normal template and pre-decides everything it reasonably can, so the only remaining action is pasting content in and hitting send — no tone choice, no length choice, no angle choice left open, because those are exactly the small decisions that get disproportionately expensive on a hard day.

contentSections.question: Put these in the order you'd actually go through to build a low-capacity version of an existing full template.
steps: Start from a full template you already use and trust
For each open blank, decide on a single default choice that would work for most uses
Rewrite the template with those defaults built in, leaving only the content itself as a blank
Save it as a separate, clearly labelled entry — not a replacement for the full version
contentSections.explanation: The low-capacity version isn't written from scratch — it's the full version with every open decision already made once, in advance, on a day with the capacity to make it thoughtfully. Keeping both versions, clearly labelled, means the right one is available on whichever kind of day actually shows up.

contentSections.body: A low-capacity library entry isn't a worse version of the full one — it's the full one with every open decision already made in advance, saved for the day deciding costs more than usual.

title: Keeping the library from rotting
description: Why a finished, working library entry isn't actually finished — and the tell (a habitual manual fix) that means it's quietly stopped earning its place.

learningObjectives.text: Diagnose a rotted library entry from a pattern of repeated manual correction
Evaluate why library entries need periodic maintenance rather than one-time authoring

contentSections.title: Set and forget doesn't work here either

contentSections.body: A small nonprofit's operations lead built a beautiful ten-entry prompt library eighteen months ago. She hasn't looked at it since. Three entries reference a grant database the org stopped using a year ago. One entry, for donor thank-you notes, has quietly been producing slightly-too-formal results for months — she's just adjusted her expectations rather than noticing the entry itself might need updating.

contentSections.scenario: The donor thank-you entry used to produce warm, specific notes. It still runs without error, but the results have felt "a little off" for months, and she's been manually editing the output every time rather than questioning the entry.
contentSections.question: What's actually happening here?

options.label: The entry has quietly stopped earning its place, and manually fixing the output every time is masking that instead of solving it
AI tools naturally degrade over time and nothing can be done
Donor thank-you notes are simply too hard for AI to draft well

feedback.masking: Right. Manually fixing the same kind of issue every single time is the tell — it means the entry itself needs revisiting, not that this is just how it is now.
feedback.degrade: AI models don't quietly degrade on their own — something specific changed (the underlying task, an updated model's behaviour, or the entry drifting from what actually works), and that's worth diagnosing rather than assuming as inevitable.
feedback.too-hard: The entry worked well when first written — the issue isn't the task's inherent difficulty, it's that something changed since then and nobody revisited the entry.

contentSections.mechanism: The reliable tell that an entry needs maintenance isn't a dramatic failure — it's exactly this pattern: a small, repeated manual fix applied every time instead of ever being traced back to the entry that keeps needing it.

contentSections.body: The tell that a library entry needs maintenance is a small manual fix you've started applying every time out of habit — that's the entry telling you it's rotted, if you're willing to notice.

title: Sharing it with someone else
description: What actually makes a shared prompt library usable by someone else — the unwritten context, not just the prompt wording.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate why raw prompt text, without context, fails to transfer usefully to another person
Write the context (purpose, trigger, assumptions) a library entry needs to be usable by someone else

contentSections.title: The knowledge that was never written down

contentSections.body: A new hire at a small design studio asks a senior colleague, "do you have any go-to prompts you use?" The colleague forwards a folder with fourteen text files, no names beyond "prompt3.txt," no notes. The new hire opens two of them, can't tell what either is for without guessing, and quietly goes back to writing everything from scratch.

What makes a library actually shareable isn't more entries or better wording — it's the context a new reader doesn't have. For each entry worth sharing: what's it for, when should someone reach for it instead of writing fresh, and what does it assume about the reader's situation that might not hold for them. That's usually one or two honest sentences, and it's the difference between a library someone can actually use and a folder of text files nobody opens twice.
Sharing a prompt library well means sharing the unwritten context along with the wording — what it's for, when to use it, what it assumes — not just the prompt text itself.

title: Build your personal prompt library
description: Assemble, template, test and label at least ten real library entries — including low-capacity versions — pulled from your own genuinely repeated work.

learningObjectives.text: Select genuinely repeated tasks worth a library entry using this module's test
Build, test and label a working personal prompt library including low-capacity versions

contentSections.body: Every lesson in this module has been building toward one artefact: a real, personal library you'll actually reach for — not a tidy example, but ten entries pulled from your own repeated work, each one tested at least once and labelled well enough that you (or someone else) could use it without guessing.

contentSections.title: Build your personal prompt library
contentSections.brief: Assemble at least ten real library entries for tasks you genuinely repeat. Each one gets tested — actually run, at least once — and gets a short note on when to use it. At least a few should have a matching low-capacity version.
contentSections.deliverable: A library of at least ten tested entries, each with a short note on when to use it, at least three of which have a paired low-capacity version.

stages.title: Inventory candidate tasks
stages.instructions: List everything you do with an AI tool at least a few times a month, or would if you had a good saved prompt for it. Apply lesson one's test to each — real recurring trigger, consistent enough shape — and keep only the ones that pass. Aim for at least ten survivors; if you're short, think across work, admin, and personal tasks, not just one category.
stages.checkpoint: You have at least ten candidate tasks that pass lesson one's repetition-and-shape test.

stages.title: Write and template each entry
stages.instructions: For each candidate, write it as either a simple saved prompt (if nothing meaningfully varies) or a full template with explicit variable slots (if it does), using lesson two's naming test — nothing left to memory.
stages.checkpoint: Every entry either has no variables (a true fixed prompt) or has every variable explicitly, visibly marked.

stages.title: Build low-capacity versions for at least three
stages.instructions: Pick at least three entries — ideally ones you'd want available even on a hard day — and write a low-capacity version that pre-decides every open choice, per lesson three.
stages.checkpoint: At least three entries have a paired low-capacity version with nothing left open to decide.

stages.title: Test every entry once and write its context note
stages.instructions: Actually run every entry once, with real content, and check the result is genuinely usable — not just plausible-looking. For each, write one or two sentences: what it's for, when to reach for it, what it assumes — per lesson five, written as if handing this to someone who's never seen your work.
stages.checkpoint: Every entry has been run at least once with real content, and has a context note a stranger could use to decide whether it applies to their situation.

rubric.criterion: At least ten entries, all genuinely repeated tasks
rubric.meets: Every entry passes lesson one's test — a real trigger and consistent shape, not a one-off saved just in case.

rubric.criterion: Variables are explicit
rubric.meets: Every entry either has no variable parts, or names every variable slot explicitly — nothing implied or left to memory.

rubric.criterion: At least three low-capacity pairs exist
rubric.meets: Three or more entries have a matching low-capacity version with every open choice pre-decided.

rubric.criterion: Every entry is tested and has a context note
rubric.meets: Each entry has actually been run once with real content, and carries a short, specific note on purpose, trigger and assumptions.

contentSections.body: A library of ten entries you'll actually reach for, each tested and labelled, is worth more than fifty you wrote once and will never find again.

questions.from: This module — A prompt library for the things you do repeatedly
questions.prompt: Why does retyping a prompt from memory each time cause inconsistent results?

options.label: Small unintentional wording differences each time genuinely change what the AI produces
The AI itself becomes unreliable over repeated use
Feedback requests are inherently too unpredictable

questions.explanation: A saved, reused prompt removes the variability that comes from reconstructing wording from memory each time.

questions.from: This module — Templates for your recurring tasks
questions.prompt: What makes a saved prompt a real template rather than just a saved prompt?

options.label: Every part of the prompt that changes between uses has its own explicitly marked variable slot
It's written in a longer, more formal style
It includes at least one example

questions.explanation: Anything left implied in a template is a variable slot quietly depending on memory — the opposite of what a template is for.

questions.from: This module — Routines for a low-capacity day

options.label: Every open choice (tone, length, angle) is pre-decided in advance, leaving nothing but pasting content in
It's simply a shorter explanation of the same choices

A subscription tier name

options.label: A consumer chat subscription doesn't provide the programmable API access an automated workflow needs
Subscriptions are always more expensive
It would have worked fine

options.label: It pays for reasoning capability the narrow, well-defined task doesn't need
Cheaper models can never be trusted

questions.explanation: Matching cost to task difficulty is the same discipline this module applies to matching a library entry's complexity to what the task actually needs.

options.label: A rate limit, expired trial credit, and a recurring monthly cap

title: Choosing a problem worth solving
description: Why a real, modestly-scoped problem you actually have makes a stronger capstone than an impressive, hypothetical one — because only a real problem lets the rest of the phase's skills mean anything.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate a candidate capstone problem for whether it's real, scoped, and personally owned

contentSections.body: Two people start this phase's capstone in the same week. One spends three days designing an elaborate multi-step agent for managing a small business's entire customer pipeline — a business they don't run, built from imagination. The other spends twenty minutes picking the actual thing that's bothered them for a year: manually reformatting a weekly volunteer schedule into three different formats for three different group chats. By the end of the phase, only one of them has something they can honestly say worked.

contentSections.scenario: A capstone candidate list: (1) "Build a general-purpose AI assistant for small businesses" (2) "Automatically flag any of my own recurring calendar conflicts before they happen" (3) "Create the ultimate AI-powered productivity system" (4) "Draft the weekly newsletter summary I currently spend 40 minutes writing by hand every Friday"
contentSections.question: Which of these are real, scoped capstone problems, versus which are too broad or not actually the author's own problem to solve?

options.label: 2 and 4 — specific, real, personally-owned, and scoped to a single task
1 and 3 — ambitious scope shows more capability
All four are equally valid capstone choices

feedback.2and4: Right. Both are specific, real, and owned by the author — a recurring calendar conflict and a genuine 40-minutes-a-week newsletter task, each small enough to actually finish and honestly measure.
feedback.1and3: "General-purpose assistant for small businesses" and "the ultimate productivity system" are both too broad to finish in this phase's scope, and neither is a problem the author necessarily has themselves — ambition here works against, not for, being able to test and measure honestly.
feedback.all: 1 and 3 fail on scope and ownership even though they sound impressive — a capstone this broad can't be meaningfully tested against real cases or measured for real benefit within the phase.

contentSections.concept: A capstone problem worth choosing is **real** (someone genuinely has it, ideally the author), **scoped** (small enough to actually finish), and **answerable** with this phase's actual tools — not chosen for how impressive it sounds.

contentSections.body: This isn't a modest-ambitions lecture — it's the same practical discipline module one applied to choosing chat versus script versus agent, now applied to choosing the problem itself. A grand, hypothetical problem can't be tested against real messy cases (lesson three) because there's no real use to test against, and it can't be honestly measured for benefit (lesson four) because there's no real before-state to compare to. A modest, real problem can be — and honestly finishing a real, if small, solution teaches more than an impressive, untested plan for a big one.
The strongest capstone problem is real, personally owned, and small enough to finish — not the one that sounds most impressive in a description.

title: Designing the approach and the checks
description: Choosing the pattern, estimating the cost, and — the step most often skipped — defining exactly what success will be checked against, all before building starts.

learningObjectives.text: Select and justify a pattern and a rough cost estimate for a real problem
Define a specific, checkable success criterion before building a solution

contentSections.title: Decide what "worked" means before you start

contentSections.body: A freelancer building a capstone to draft client invoices' descriptions automatically skips straight to building. Three weeks later, someone asks her "did it work?" She pauses. It runs. It produces text. Whether it's actually better than what she did before — faster, more accurate, less annoying — she genuinely can't say, because she never decided what "better" would look like before she started.

This module's design step borrows directly from three earlier lessons in this phase: choosing the **pattern** (module one) that fits the problem's actual shape, roughly **costing** it (module three) before committing real time, and — the piece most often skipped — deciding, in writing, **what success will be checked against**, the same way a lab rubric is written before the lab starts, not invented afterward to match whatever got built.

contentSections.intro: Design the approach for: a small nonprofit's volunteer coordinator wants weekly shift reminders drafted automatically instead of writing each one by hand.

fields.prompt: Given this repeats weekly with a consistent shape and doesn't need much individual judgement per volunteer, which pattern fits (module one)?
options: A script/automation with an AI step for personalising the message
A full autonomous agent managing volunteer relationships
fields.correctValue: A script/automation with an AI step for personalising the message

feedback.A script/automation with an AI step for: Right — a weekly, consistent-shape task with limited judgement needed fits a script well, per module one's simplicity test.
feedback.A full autonomous agent managing volunte: This is more machinery than a weekly reminder message needs — the task doesn't require multi-step autonomous decision-making.

fields.prompt: Given roughly 30 volunteers, weekly, short messages — is a rough cost check (module three) worth doing before building?
options: Yes — even a quick estimate catches whether this is genuinely cheap or a surprise waiting to happen
No — it's obviously going to be free
fields.correctValue: Yes — even a quick estimate catches whether this is genuinely cheap or a surprise waiting to happen

feedback.Yes — even a quick estimate catches whet: Right — even when a cost is likely small, a five-minute estimate is cheap insurance against an unexamined assumption, per module three.
feedback.No — it's obviously going to be free: Nothing is "obviously free" until it's actually been estimated — this is exactly the assumption module three warned against skipping.

fields.prompt: What's a genuinely checkable definition of success here, rather than a feeling?
options: "Saves at least 20 minutes a week, and volunteers report the reminders feel just as personal as before"
fields.correctValue: "Saves at least 20 minutes a week, and volunteers report the reminders feel just as personal as before"

feedback.\"Saves at least 20 minutes a week, and: Right — specific, checkable on two fronts (time and a real signal from real recipients), not a vague impression.
feedback.\"It should feel more efficient\": This is exactly the vague, uncheckable target that leaves someone unable to answer "did it work?" three weeks later.

contentSections.synthesis: A sound capstone design names its pattern with a reason, estimates its cost even when the estimate is likely small, and defines success as something specific enough to actually check afterward — all three decided before building starts, not reconstructed afterward to match whatever got built.

contentSections.body: Decide the pattern, the rough cost, and what "it worked" specifically means — all three, before you build anything — or you'll be stuck with a feeling instead of an answer.

title: Building it and testing on real cases
description: Why testing has to include deliberately messy, real input — not just the clean examples the builder happened to write — before a capstone is trustworthy.

learningObjectives.text: Test a built solution against genuinely messy real cases, not just self-written tidy examples
Apply deterministic-check placement to catch malformed input before it reaches a judgement-requiring step

contentSections.title: The messiest real case you can find

contentSections.body: A capstone project drafts personalised responses to a community forum's most common repeated questions. Its builder tests it against three questions he wrote himself, all clearly phrased, all matching the exact topics he expected. It works beautifully. He turns it on. The first real question is four rambling sentences that eventually, buried in the middle, asks something completely different from what any of his three test questions covered.

Testing on real cases means specifically seeking out — not avoiding — the input that's most likely to break something: the longest, most ambiguous, most oddly-phrased real example you can find, plus at least one case with something missing or malformed, exactly as module two's failure-handling lesson described. If the capstone is something only you will use, this can be as simple as digging through your own real, messy history for the actual worst example, rather than writing convenient new ones.

This is also where module two's placement principle pays off directly: if a deterministic check (is this even a valid input, has this already been handled) sits before the AI-driven part of the build, most malformed cases get caught and handled predictably before they ever reach the part of the system making a judgement call — which is exactly what real testing is checking for.

contentSections.question: Before moving on: if the forum-response capstone had a simple rule-based check in front of the AI step — "is this actually a question, or something else entirely (spam, a greeting, a moderator note)" — would that have caught the rambling four-sentence question that confused it?
contentSections.answer: Not necessarily on its own — the rambling question was a real question, just awkwardly phrased, so a simple is-this-a-question filter wouldn't have screened it out. That's an honest limit worth naming: deterministic pre-checks catch clearly invalid input well, but a genuinely messy real question still has to be handled by whatever's doing the judgement-requiring work, which is exactly why deliberately testing with messy-but-valid input matters as much as testing with invalid input.
contentSections.hint: The rambling question wasn't invalid or malformed — it was a real question, just phrased in an unexpected way. Does a validity filter catch that?

contentSections.body: Testing on real cases means deliberately seeking out the messiest real example available, not writing three convenient ones and calling it done.

title: Measuring the actual benefit
description: Why a strong feeling that something helped isn't the same as a genuine, checkable measurement — and the simple numbers (timed comparison, correction rate, actual use) that turn one into the other.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a genuine, checkable measurement of benefit from a restated feeling
Design a simple before/after measurement for a real capstone outcome

contentSections.title: Feeling faster isn't the same as being faster

contentSections.body: A small retailer's owner is confident her new AI-drafted product description tool saves her real time. When asked to estimate how much, she says "a lot." When actually timed — writing one description the old way, then one the new way including reviewing and lightly editing the AI's draft — the difference is four minutes. Real, worth keeping, but nowhere near "a lot," and worth knowing precisely rather than vaguely.

Measuring actual benefit doesn't require anything elaborate — it means picking one or two concrete, checkable numbers before declaring success, in the spirit of module three's honest arithmetic: a timed before/after comparison, a correction rate (how many outputs needed real fixing before being usable), or a simple count of "did I actually use this, this week" over a couple of weeks. Whichever number, the test is the same: could someone else look at what you measured and see the same thing you're claiming, or is it really just a strong impression dressed up as a result?
A genuine measurement is something a sceptical friend could be shown and verify — "it feels better," however confidently stated, isn't that.

title: Writing up what you'd tell someone else
description: The short, honest write-up — problem, approach and why, cost, measured benefit, and a genuine verdict on ongoing use — that makes a capstone legible to your future self and to anyone else.

learningObjectives.text: Write an honest, specific account of a project's problem, approach, cost, measured benefit and ongoing use

contentSections.title: The write-up is for future you too

contentSections.body: A year after building a small automation for tracking freelance invoices, its builder gets asked by a friend starting a similar business: "how did you set that up, and was it worth it?" She has nothing to point to — no notes on why she chose that approach, what it cost, or whether she actually still uses it (she does, mostly, though one part quietly broke months ago and she just started doing that bit by hand again without really noticing the shift).

The write-up this lesson asks for isn't a polished case study — it's the same honest context module four's sharing lesson described, applied to the whole capstone rather than one library entry: what problem was real, what approach was chosen and why (against the neighbouring alternatives, per module one), roughly what it cost (per module three), what was actually measured as the benefit (per lesson four), and a genuinely honest verdict on whether it's still in use. That last part matters most, and is the part people are most tempted to skip or soften.
An honest write-up — including admitting if something quietly stopped working — is worth more to your future self and to anyone else than a polished account that only tells the flattering half.

title: Critique seven capstone designs including your own
description: Seven drills applying this phase's full capstone discipline — problem choice, upfront checks, real-case testing, genuine measurement, and honest write-ups — to designs including your own.

learningObjectives.text: Critique a capstone design against problem-choice, testing and measurement criteria at speed

contentSections.body: Seven drills across this whole phase's capstone skills: choosing a real problem, designing checks up front, testing against messy cases, measuring genuine benefit, and writing an honest account — including critiquing designs that aren't your own. Nothing here is timed.
If a drill needed a hint, that's worth watching for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Deliver the capstone
description: Choose a real problem, design it with checks defined up front, build and test it against messy real cases, measure the genuine benefit, and write an honest account — the whole phase's discipline, applied start to finish.

learningObjectives.text: Design, build and test a capstone solution against real, messy cases
Measure a capstone's actual benefit and report it honestly

contentSections.body: This is where the whole phase lands: not a bigger exercise, but the same real discipline — choose, design, build, test, measure, write up honestly — applied to a problem that actually matters to you, start to finish.

contentSections.title: Deliver the capstone
contentSections.brief: Choose one real problem of your own. Design an approach with success checks defined before you build. Build it, and test it against real, messy cases — not just tidy ones you wrote yourself. Measure whether it actually helped, with a real number, not a feeling. Then write up an honest account, including anything that didn't work.
contentSections.deliverable: A working solution, a description of how it was verified (including at least one deliberately messy test case), a genuine measured result, and an honest write-up covering the problem, approach and why, cost, what was measured, and current status.

stages.title: Choose and design
stages.instructions: Pick a real, scoped, personally-owned problem per lesson one. Using lesson two, name the pattern (with a one-line defence against a neighbouring option), a rough cost estimate, and a specific, checkable definition of success — all before building anything.
stages.checkpoint: You have a written problem statement, a defended pattern choice, a cost estimate, and a specific success definition.

stages.title: Build it
stages.instructions: Build the solution using whatever pattern you chose — a template, a script, an automation, or a combination. Keep any deterministic checks placed before AI-driven judgement steps, per module two.
stages.checkpoint: The solution runs and produces output on at least one real input.

stages.title: Test on real, messy cases
stages.instructions: Run it against at least one clean real case and, deliberately, the messiest or most awkward real case you can find or construct, plus a case with something missing or malformed. Note what happened each time.
stages.checkpoint: At least one deliberately messy or malformed case has been tested, with the result recorded — not just clean cases.

stages.title: Measure the actual benefit
stages.instructions: Using lesson four, produce one real, checkable number — a timed before/after comparison, a correction rate, or an actual-use count — rather than a general impression.
stages.checkpoint: A specific, checkable measurement exists, not a restated feeling.

stages.title: Write the honest account
stages.instructions: Write the short version from lesson five: the problem, the approach and why, the rough cost, what was measured, and a genuinely honest verdict on whether you're actually using it — including admitting if something didn't work or you've already stopped.
stages.checkpoint: The write-up states an honest current-use verdict, not just a summary of what was built.

rubric.criterion: The problem is real, scoped, and personally owned
rubric.meets: A specific real problem is named, with a real person (possibly the author) who has it and a scope that was actually finishable.

rubric.criterion: Success was defined before building
rubric.meets: A specific, checkable success definition exists and was written before the build stage, not reconstructed afterward.

rubric.criterion: Testing included a deliberately messy case
rubric.meets: At least one genuinely messy or malformed real case was tested, not only clean self-written examples.

rubric.criterion: Benefit was measured, not just felt
rubric.meets: A specific, checkable number (time, correction rate, or usage count) backs the claim of benefit.

rubric.criterion: The write-up is honest
rubric.meets: The account includes cost, measured benefit, and a genuine current-use verdict — including any honest admission of what didn't work.

contentSections.body: The whole phase comes down to this: pick something real, decide what success means before you start, test it against the mess, measure it honestly, and say so in writing — including the parts that didn't go perfectly.

questions.from: This module — Choosing a problem worth solving
questions.prompt: What makes a capstone problem worth choosing?

options.label: It's real, personally owned, and scoped small enough to actually finish
It sounds impressive when described to someone else
It uses the most sophisticated pattern from the phase

questions.explanation: A grand, hypothetical problem can't be genuinely tested or measured, since there's no real before-state or real user to check against.

questions.from: This module — Designing the approach and the checks
questions.prompt: What's the step most often skipped before building, that leaves someone unable to say whether their capstone actually worked?

options.label: Defining a specific, checkable success criterion before building starts
Choosing the most powerful available AI model
Getting a second opinion from a friend

questions.explanation: Without a success definition decided up front, "did it work" collapses into an unverifiable feeling.

questions.from: This module — Building it and testing on real cases
questions.prompt: Why does testing only against self-written, tidy examples fail to prove a capstone is trustworthy?

options.label: It doesn't reveal how the build handles messy, unexpected real input, which is what real use will actually produce
Self-written tests are always technically invalid
It doesn't matter — passing any test is sufficient

questions.explanation: This is the same gap module two's no-code lesson named — a convincing demo doesn't prove resilience to real, messy input.

questions.from: This module — Measuring the actual benefit
questions.prompt: Why isn't "it definitely feels faster" a sufficient claim of benefit?

options.label: It's an impression, not a checkable measurement — a real timed comparison could confirm or contradict it
Feelings are never useful information
AI-assisted tasks are always slower in practice

questions.explanation: A genuine measurement is something a sceptical friend could be shown and verify — an impression, however confident, isn't that.

questions.from: Previous module — Your Own AI System
questions.prompt: What makes a saved prompt a real template rather than just a saved prompt?

options.label: Every part of the prompt that changes between uses has its own explicitly marked variable slot
It's written in a longer, more formal style
It includes at least one example

questions.explanation: This carries into the capstone's own design step whenever a template-based approach is chosen.

questions.from: Previous module — Your Own AI System
questions.prompt: What's the reliable tell that a library entry (or, by extension, any built solution) has quietly rotted?

options.label: A small manual fix applied by hand, the same way, every single time it's used
It's been used more than fifty times
It hasn't been opened in a year

questions.explanation: The same tell applies directly to a capstone's honest write-up — noting a recurring manual patch is exactly the kind of honesty lesson five asks for.

questions.from: Previous module — Your Own AI System
questions.prompt: What actually makes a shared prompt library, or a written account of a project, usable by someone else?

options.label: Explicit context — what it's for, when to use it, what it assumes — not just the content itself
Sharing as many entries or details as possible
Formatting it attractively

questions.explanation: This is the direct basis for the capstone write-up's own standard in lesson five.

questions.from: Previous module — Your Own AI System
questions.prompt: What structurally distinguishes a low-capacity library entry from its full version?

options.label: Every open choice is pre-decided in advance, leaving nothing but pasting content in
It's just a shorter explanation of the same choices
It uses a cheaper AI model

questions.explanation: Retained from the previous module as background for anyone whose capstone touches their personal library.

questions.from: Older module — Beyond the Chat Box
questions.prompt: What's the practical rule for choosing among chat, embedded feature, script, and agent?

options.label: Climb the ladder only as far as the task's actual volume and judgement needs require
Always start with the most powerful, most autonomous option
Agents are always the best choice for anything repeated

questions.explanation: This governs the capstone's own pattern choice in lesson two — proportionality, not sophistication.

questions.from: Older module — What It Costs
questions.prompt: What's the correct shape of a cost estimate for a workflow?

options.label: (volume × input tokens × input price) + (volume × output tokens × output price), calculated separately
Volume × a single combined per-token price
A flat guess based on how the workflow feels

questions.explanation: This is exactly the calculation the capstone's design stage asks for before building.
